subject: Simple Hierarchical model gets incorrect answer

messages.author: bbb3e72cd6187a0f
messages.subject: Simple Hierarchical model gets incorrect answer
parts:
Hi there,

I have the following model:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;                // number of halos
    vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // measured halo masses
    vector<lower=0>[N] sd_dex;     // uncertainty in halo masses (dex)
    real<lower=0> V;               // Volume of the survey

    // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
    vector<lower=0>[2] hs_bounds;             // Bounds of logHs
    vector<lower=-2,upper=0>[2] alpha_bounds; // Bounds of alpha
    vector<lower=0>[2] beta_bounds;           // Bounds of beta
    vector<lower=0>[2] mmin_bounds;           // Bounds of log_mmin
    vector<lower=0>[2] mtrue_bounds;          // Bounds of log_mtrue
    vector[2] lnA_bounds;                     // Bounds of lnA

}

parameters {
    real<lower=hs_bounds[1],upper=hs_bounds[2]> logHs;               // Characteristic halo mass
    real<lower=alpha_bounds[1],upper=alpha_bounds[2]> alpha;         // Power-law slope
    real<lower=beta_bounds[1],upper=beta_bounds[2]> beta;            // Cut-off parameter
    real<lower=mmin_bounds[1],upper=mmin_bounds[2]> log_mmin;        // Truncation mass
    vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_bounds[2]>[N] log_mtrue;       // True mass estimates
}

transformed parameters {
    real lnA;
    real raw_lnA;
    real gzx;

    gzx <- gammainc((alpha+1)/beta,exp(log10()*(log_mmin-logHs)*beta));
    raw_lnA <- log(N) - log10()*logHs - log(gzx);
    lnA <- raw_lnA - log(V);
}

model {
    vector[N] y;
    y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
    y ~ truncated_logGGD(logHs, alpha, beta, raw_lnA, gzx);
    for (i in 1:N) log_mtrue[i] ~ normal(log_m_meas[i],sd_dex[i]) T[0,];
}


The code also contains the definition of a function for the truncated_logGGD_log, which I am confident is giving the correct numerical result (from tests outside of Stan). I didn't include it because it distracts from everything else. In short, the truncated_logGGD is the pdf of a generalised-gamma distribution truncated at mmin defined in log10-space. For intuition, this pdf looks like a decreasing power-law up to the value of about logHs, after which it cuts off exponentially. In fact, I can do better than that. Here's a picture of it:



The green and red lines are the truncated GGD (green is the intrinsic parameters of the distribution, red is the estimated).

The input data, log_m_meas, is generated by choosing a value of mmin (in the case above, it is very close to 10^12), generating "intrinsic" data by sampling the truncated_logGGD (the pink region shows this intrinsic distribution), and then applying "measurement uncertainty" by choosing a measured value from a normal distribution with mean given by the intrinsic value, and uncertainty sd_dex[i] (this value is derived from an entirely separate model, and we just take it as "known" in this application).

The above stan model should thus be the inverse generative model (I hope). However, you can see clearly that the parameters are wrong, and not by just a little bit.

So, I had a bit of a deeper look. I calculated the MLE in a simple case using the intrinsic values and no sd_dex (i.e. a simple non-hierarchical model), and then put these parameters back into the full hierarchical model to get an estimate of the log-prob of what I would expect to be very close to the right answer. I also grabbed the MLE (estimated as the iteration with highest log-prob) from the full hierarchical run.

The results were such that (expected - hierarchical) = -94.8. That is, the mode of the hierarchical run was of high probability than the expected answer. That makes sense, because that's where the sampler ended up.

But then I wondered which part of the calculation favours the "wrong" solution, so I printed out the probability before any of the likelihood calculations, after the logGGD call and then after the normal() call. I got the following:

                 |   Hier.    |  Expect.  | Diff.
-----------------|------------|-----------|--------
Before anything: |  -4102.91  |  -3036.69 | ~-1070
After GGD:       |   11040.7  |  11018.7  | ~1100
After Normal:    |   9947.09  |  10041.9  | ~-100

Basically, if the "before anything" row didn't exist, the model would behave more as I expected -- the expected would be more likely. As far as I can understand, the "before anything" row comes about because of the transformation of parameters to unconstrained space, am I right? I was just wondering why this should mean my model ends up in the "wrong place". As in, if no transformation was applied, and I used the constrained parameters directly, my model would end up in the place I expect it. So why should it change when the transformation is applied? Am I missing something in my model which would account for this?

Thanks for any help!

Regards,
Steven

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple Hierarchical model gets incorrect answer
parts:
Why have a lower=0 bound on the log scale?
And we don't genrally recommend bounds like (-2, 0)
unless the parameter is physically constrained to (-2, 0).
Otherwise, you can bias the posterior means considerably by
truncating non-negligible probability mass.

In general, you just code the generative model directly
in Stan and Stan does the inversion---you shouldn't try
to code the inversion directly unless you have analytical
steps (which can save time and make the statistical mixing
more efficient).

The MLE is not the iteration with the highest log density.
Often the MLE isn't in the typical set at all, so you won't
get anywhere near it (e.g., try sampling from a 20-dimensional
unit normal exactly and see how close you get to zero, the MLE).
What you want to be doing is checking posterior interval
calibration (coverage, say, of the 50% intervals).

Also, just measuring by the log density won't tell you much.

I'm afraid I don't understand this truncated density---maybe
someone else could help?

- Bob

parts: Thanks for your fast response Bob.

On Saturday, 27 August 2016 03:12:18 UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Why have a lower=0 bound on the log scale?
You're right, I've removed that now, not that it should make much difference.

And we don't genrally recommend bounds like (-2, 0)
unless the parameter is physically constrained to (-2, 0).

What do you suggest then? I wanted to (at least initially) use a uniform prior, but of course it's improper to use an unbounded uniform prior. I know alpha is ~-1.87 and should have a very tight constraint. It will never be greater than -1.5 and there's reason to expect it to be constrained above -2 (though technically it could be lower). Typically I find that it's -1.87 +- 0.02 or so. Given that kind of range, would these bounds still be a source of bias? I've run it again (see below) with more generous bounds to check for myself.

Otherwise, you can bias the posterior means considerably by
truncating non-negligible probability mass.

In general, you just code the generative model directly
in Stan and Stan does the inversion---you shouldn't try
to code the inversion directly unless you have analytical
steps (which can save time and make the statistical mixing
more efficient).

Sorry, yes I used the generative model directly. I mean, I generate the data by choosing the parameters, sampling from the truncated_logGGD with those parameters to get log_mtrue, then sampling from a normal to get log_m_meas. That's directly what I have in my model.

The MLE is not the iteration with the highest log density.
Often the MLE isn't in the typical set at all, so you won't
get anywhere near it (e.g., try sampling from a 20-dimensional
unit normal exactly and see how close you get to zero, the MLE).
What you want to be doing is checking posterior interval
calibration (coverage, say, of the 50% intervals).

Okay, fair enough. So, are you saying that even though the expected solution had a lower likelihood than another region in my chains, that it's possible that the chain would centre around the expected solution anyway?
Also, just measuring by the log density won't tell you much.
In a couple of re-runs below I show the parameter intervals instead. Is this better?

I'm afraid I don't understand this truncated density---maybe
someone else could help?

That's fine. I'm confident that the truncated density is doing what it's supposed to.
 
- Bob


So, I ran again with the following model (note I just took out some of the bounds on log parameters):

data {
    int<lower=0> N;                // number of halos
vector[N] log_m_meas; // measured halo masses

vector<lower=0>[N] sd_dex;     // uncertainty in halo masses (dex)
    real<lower=0> V;               // Volume of the survey

    // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS

vector[2] hs_bounds;             // Bounds of logHs
    vector[2] alpha_bounds;          // Bounds of alpha
vector<lower=0>[2] beta_bounds;  // Bounds of beta

vector[2] mmin_bounds;           // Bounds of log_mmin
    vector[2] mtrue_bounds;          // Bounds of log_mtrue

vector[2] lnA_bounds;            // Bounds of lnA
}

parameters {
    real<lower=hs_bounds[1],upper=hs_bounds[2]> logHs;               // Characteristic halo mass
    real<lower=alpha_bounds[1],upper=alpha_bounds[2]> alpha;         // Power-law slope
    real<lower=beta_bounds[1],upper=beta_bounds[2]> beta;            // Cut-off parameter
    real<lower=mmin_bounds[1],upper=mmin_bounds[2]> log_mmin;        // Truncation mass
    vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_bounds[2]>[N] log_mtrue;       // True mass estimates
}

transformed parameters {
    real lnA;
    real raw_lnA;
    real gzx;

    gzx <- gammainc((alpha+1)/beta,exp(log10()*(log_mmin-logHs)*beta));
    raw_lnA <- log(N) - log10()*logHs - log(gzx);
    lnA <- raw_lnA - log(V);
}

model {
    vector[N] y;
    y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
    y ~ truncated_logGGD(logHs, alpha, beta, raw_lnA, gzx);

log_m_meas ~ normal(log_mtrue,sd_dex);
}


I first ran with the following data [this is the same as I used in my results for the last post] (note I constrain alpha, i.e. the power-law slope of the function to (-1.99,-1.7)):

{'N': 5078, 
 'V': 1190658.039618655, 
 'alpha_bounds': (-1.99, -1.7), 
 'beta_bounds': (0.4, 1.2), 
 'hs_bounds': (13, 15.5), 
 'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37), 
 'log_m_meas': array([ 13.35251163, 11.78469724, 12.01253925, ..., 12.72611462, 14.18542692, 12.40310497]), 
 'mmin_bounds': (10, 14), 
 'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),  # Note: only the upper bound here is actually used.
 'sd_dex': array([ 0.63660784, 0.79483786, 0.79483786, ..., 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 ])}

The Stan summary is

                  mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
logHs            14.61    0.02   0.27  14.15  14.42  14.59  14.77  15.21  280.0   1.01

and the input values were 

{'alpha': -1.8682714014860426,  ## outside 50% coverage
 'beta': 0.6999588565297955,    ## outside 50% coverage

 'log_mmin': 12.04004004        ## just outside 50% coverage
}

The traceplot looks like:





I then ran it again, with the following data (note the relaxation of several bounds):

{'N': 5046,
 'V': 1190658.039618655,
 'alpha_bounds': (-3, -1),
 'beta_bounds': (0.2, 2.0),
 'hs_bounds': (12, 15.05),
 'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37),
 'log_m_meas': array([ 12.64310298,  11.64157076,  12.23913006, ...,  12.24778487,
         11.71975052,  13.23577041]),
 'mmin_bounds': (10, 14),
 'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),
 'sd_dex': array([ 0.8705571 ,  0.7411142 ,  0.79483786, ...,  0.79483786,
         0.79483786,  0.66539496])}

and get the following results:

                  mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
logHs            14.27    0.03   0.49  12.63  14.23  14.45  14.56  14.64  278.0    1.0
alpha            -1.74  7.1e-3    0.1  -1.88  -1.81  -1.76  -1.69  -1.48  209.0   1.01
beta              1.04    0.02   0.51   0.26   0.58    1.0   1.48   1.95  449.0    1.0
log_mmin         12.02  1.9e-3   0.03  11.97   12.0  12.02  12.03  12.06  190.0   1.01


Now logHs is within range, and so is beta (on account of its range being very large). But alpha is way off.  While running these, I noticed one interesting thing: if logHs is larger than max(log_mtrue), its effect plateau's in terms of its correlation with beta. That is, if the scale where the exponential cut-off happens is outside the range of masses, then it doesn't matter what beta is at all. That's why I've kept logHs bounded to ~15.

I ran the same model but setting the log_mtrue to the actual intrinsic masses (so no hierarchical model) and as a comparison I get the following plot (blue is the constrained model):


You can see the offset of alpha clearly. Do you think I'm doing everything right but perhaps there's just not enough data?

Thanks again,
Steven

and get the following results:

                  mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
logHs            14.27    0.03   0.49  12.63  14.23  14.45  14.56  14.64  278.0    1.0

Now logHs is within range, and so is beta (on account of its range being very large). But alpha is way off.  While running these, I noticed one interesting thing: if logHs is larger than max(log_mtrue), its effect plateau's in terms of its correlation with beta. That is, if the scale where the exponential cut-off happens is outside the range of masses, then it doesn't matter what beta is at all. That's why I've kept logHs bounded to ~15.

You can see the offset of alpha clearly. Do you think I'm doing everything right but perhaps there's just not enough data?
